reports.text: ARCHIVE: Groups in the Israel lobby exert significant leverage over the executive branch. Influence over the executive branch derives in part from the impact pro-Israel voters and donors have on presidential elections. Pro-Israel donors are a small part of the population. But they make large campaign donations to candidates from both parties. Hamilton Jordan was presidential adviser and former White House Chief of Staff. He wrote in a confidential memo to President Jimmy Carter: "Wherever there is major political fundraising in this country, you will find American Jews playing a significant role." The Washington Post once estimated that Democratic presidential candidates "depend on Jewish supporters to supply as much as 60 percent of the money raised from private sources." Other estimates are lower. But pro-Israel contributions form a substantial share, between 20 and 50 percent, of the contributions made to the Democratic party and its presidential candidates. Israel is not the only issue that inspires these contributions. But candidates who are perceived as hostile, or even indifferent, to Israel run the risk of seeing some of these funds go to their opponents. Pro-Israel voters also have high turnout rates. They are concentrated in key states like California, Florida, Illinois, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania. This increases their weight in determining who becomes president. In close races this vote can tip the balance in key states. Jeffrey Helmreich of the Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs wrote that "American Jewish voters maintain the potential to be the decisive factor in national election results... American Jews wield power through their high concentration in key states and their tendency to behave as a swing vote." Because this vote matters in close elections, presidential candidates go to considerable lengths to cultivate support. Candidates are especially eager to appeal to AIPAC and other organizations in the lobby. They know that the seal of approval from these prominent organizations will facilitate fund-raising and encourage higher turnout on their behalf. Gaining and retaining that support means backing Israel down the line. This happens even though Israel strategic value has declined. It also happens even though some Israeli actions, like the continued effort to colonize the Occupied Territories, are at odds with stated US policy. So the lobby uses American campaign money and American election mechanics to make US presidents back Israel. This happens against America own stated policy. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: AIPAC traditional tactics to influence Congress also enable the lobby to put pressure on the executive branch. This happens when the executive takes actions considered not in Israel interest. When that happens the president or cabinet official is likely to get a hard-hitting letter from one or both houses of Congress. The letter is signed by most of its members. President Gerald Ford got such a letter in 1975 when he threatened a reassessment of US-Israeli relations. President Bush got a similar letter in April 2002 when he briefly sought to pressure Israel to end a large-scale military incursion in the Occupied Territories. The lopsided percentage of signatories for each of these letters is eloquent testimony to AIPAC ability to twist arms. Senator Daniel Inouye (D-HI) commented after signing the letter to Ford in 1975: "It is easier to sign one letter than to answer 5000." Senator John Culver (D-IA) later admitted: "The pressure was just too great. I caved." Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice felt the same pressure. She sought to restart the peace process by visiting the Middle East in March 2007. Just before her departure Rice received an AIPAC-sponsored letter signed by seventy-nine senators. The letter urged her to avoid contact with the new Palestinian unity government until it recognized Israel, renounced terror, and agreed to abide by Israeli-Palestinian agreements. Former Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger once told AIPAC Tom Dine: "Dine, I deal with you because you could hurt me." AIPAC bills itself as America Pro-Israel Lobby. It has an almost unchallenged hold on Congress. One of the three main branches of the American government is firmly committed to supporting Israel. Open debate about US policy toward Israel does not occur there even though that policy has important consequences for the entire world. Senator Ernest Hollings (D-SC) noted as he was leaving office in 2004: "You cant have an Israeli policy other than what AIPAC gives you around here." Another senator speaking on condition of anonymity told a Washington Post reporter in 1991: "My colleagues think AIPAC is a very, very powerful organization that is ruthless, and very, very alert. Eighty percent of the senators here roll their eyes on some of the votes. They know that what they are doing isnt what they really believe is right, but why fight on a situation where they are liable to get beat up on?" Former Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon once told an American audience: "When people ask me how they can help Israel, I tell them—Help AIPAC." His successor Ehud Olmert agrees remarking: "Thank God we have AIPAC, the greatest supporter and friend we have in the whole world." Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: AIPAC influence on Capitol Hill goes beyond campaign money. Lobbying groups exercise influence by providing a legislative subsidy to sympathetic lawmakers. They supply overworked staffs with direct assistance in analyzing issues, framing legislation, and offering talking points and speeches. Every member of Congress receives AIPAC biweekly newsletter Near East Report. AIPAC personnel are also available to help staffers when issues affecting Israel arise. Douglas Bloomfield was a former AIPAC staff member. He said "It is common for members of Congress and their staffs to turn to AIPAC first when they need information, before calling the Library of Congress, the Congressional Research Service, committee staff or administration experts." More important he notes that AIPAC is "often called upon to draft speeches, work on legislation, advise on tactics, perform research, collect co-sponsors and marshal votes." To seal the deal an AIPAC sister organization funds free congressional trips to Israel. The group is called American Israel Education Foundation (AIEF). These junkets burnish a legislator pro-Israel credentials and facilitate fund-raising. They also expose him or her to policy preferences and basic worldview of Israel leaders. About 10 percent of all congressional trips overseas are to Israel. Israel is but one of nearly two hundred countries in the world. Center for Public Integrity reports that AIEF spent nearly $1 million on these visits from January 2000 to mid-2005. AIPAC and other Jewish groups lobbied hard and successfully to make sure new ethics rules did not interfere with these visits. The rules were enacted after Jack Abramoff and Tom DeLay scandals. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: AIPAC and pro-Israel PACs focus on more than getting Israel-friendly candidates elected. They have also had notable success turning politicians who have been critical of Israel into steadfast supporters. Former Senator Jesse Helms (R-NC) was an outspoken critic of the US foreign aid program for much of his career. This meant he also opposed giving substantial aid to Israel. In 1984 Helms was in a hard-fought and expensive race for reelection against James Hunt, the popular governor of North Carolina. AIPAC saw an opportunity to put a formidable enemy out of business. It channeled large amounts of campaign money to Hunt, who came within a hair of winning. Helms got the message. He traveled to Israel the following year. He had his picture taken with a yarmulke on his head kissing the Western Wall. The same trip also produced a picture of the senator with Ariel Sharon for his office wall. More important Helms became a vocal supporter of Israel and remained one until his retirement in 2002. One sees a similar evolution on the part of Senator Hillary Clinton. Her support for Palestinian statehood in 1998 and public embrace of Suha Arafat, wife of Yasser Arafat, in 1999 provoked strong criticism from groups in the lobby. Clinton became an ardent defender of Israel once she began running for office herself. She now gets strong backing including financial support from pro-Israel organizations and individuals. After Clinton appeared at a pro-Israel rally in July 2006 she expressed strong support for Israel highly destructive war against Lebanon. Helen Freedman was executive director of the hard-line Americans for a Safe Israel. She declared "I thought her remarks were very good, especially in light of her history, and we cant forget her kiss to Suha." Pro-Israel PACs contributed more than $30,000 to Clinton 2006 reelection campaign. The Forward reported in January 2007 that Clinton was "expected to snare the lions share of the Jewish community substantial political donations in the race for the 2008 Democratic Presidential nomination." Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: AIPAC helps candidates who support its agenda and works against those who do not. Over three decades it helped defeat a number of politicians it considered unfriendly to Israel. Paul Findley (R-IL) had served eleven terms in Congress. In 1982 wealthy Chicago businessman and former AIPAC President Robert Asher helped recruit and vet an Illinois attorney, Richard Durbin, to run against Findley. Durbin had never held elected office. Asher later said "I probed [Durbin] views... I wanted to make sure we were supporting someone who was not only against Paul Findley but also a friend of Israel. He beat Findley with a lot of help from Jews, in-state and out-of-state. Now, how did the Jewish money find him? I traveled around the country talking about how we had the opportunity to defeat someone unfriendly to Israel. And the gates opened." Asher sent a letter to donors calling the election the "best chance" to remove a "dangerous enemy of Israel" from Congress. Durbin received $104,325 from 31 different pro-Israel PACs. Other Illinois congressional candidates got about $3,700 on average from the same groups. Durbin narrowly beat Findley. In 2002 Mayer "Bubba" Mitchell, a member of the Gang of Four that guides AIPAC policy making, used similar tactics to oust Congressman Earl Hilliard (D-AL). Hilliard opponent got financial help from AIPAC supporters across the country. Charles Percy (R-IL) had a generally pro-Israel voting record. But he declined to sign AIPAC-sponsored "Letter of 76" protesting President Ford threatened reassessment of US Middle East policy in 1975. He also called PLO leader Yasser Arafat more "moderate" than some other Palestinian terrorists. Percy opponents in both primary and general election in 1984 got large sums from pro-Israel PACs. A businessman from California, Michael Goland, who was also a major contributor to AIPAC, spent $1.1 million on anti-Percy advertising in Illinois. Goland was later convicted of making illegal campaign contributions in 1986 California Senate race. Tom Dine of AIPAC boasted after Percy narrow defeat: "All the Jews in America, from coast to coast, gathered to oust Percy. And the American politicians—those who hold public positions now, and those who aspire—got the message." Roger Jepson (R-IA) was targeted after he agreed to support the 1981 sale of AWACS aircraft to Saudi Arabia. This came after a personal plea from President Ronald Reagan. Jepson opponent in 1984 Senate race, Democrat Tom Harkin, received more than $100,000 in pro-Israel PAC money. Jepson lost his seat. Senator Alan Cranston (D-CA) later said Jepson fate "has sort of struck terror into the hearts of senators about switching" on Middle East votes. Adlai Stevenson (D-IL) ran for governor of Illinois in 1982. He first ran afoul of pro-Israel groups in 1980 when he introduced an amendment to reduce foreign aid to Israel if it did not stop building settlements. The amendment was easily defeated, gaining only seven votes. One reluctant opponent, Senator Quentin Burdick (D-ND), told him "Sorry, Adlai, but I am up for reelection." When Stevenson ran for governor two years later campaign contributions dried up and went to his opponent. According to Stevenson he and his wife "were reviled as anti-Semitic. Some in the press turned hostile. Jewish Democratic Committeemen wilted under pressure." Stevenson was narrowly defeated. He later said "the lobby made the difference in that election many times over." Cynthia McKinney (D-GA) was defeated in 2002 with AIPAC help. She returned to office in 2004 but was again defeated in 2006. Hank Johnson, her victorious opponent in 2006 Democratic primary, received at least $34,000 from seven pro-Israel PACs. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: AIPAC President Howard Friedman told the organization members in August 2006: "AIPAC meets with every candidate running for Congress. These candidates receive in-depth briefings to help them completely understand the complexities of Israel predicament and that of the Middle East as a whole. We even ask each candidate to author a position paper on their views of the U.S.-Israel relationship—so it is clear where they stand on the subject." Tom Hayden was antiwar figure who ran for a seat in California Assembly in early 1980s. He explains how he won support from local power broker Michael Berman on condition that he would always be a "good friend to Israel." Hayden won the election. He notes that he "had to be certified kosher, not once but over and over again. The certifiers were the elites, beginning with rabbis and heads of the multiple mainstream Jewish organizations... An important vetting role was held as well by... [AIPAC], a group closely associated with official parties in Israel. When necessary, Israeli ambassadors, counsels general and other officials would intervene with statements declaring someone a friend of Israel." Harry Lonsdale was Democratic candidate who ran unsuccessfully against Senator Mark Hatfield (R-OR) in 1990. He described his own visit to AIPAC headquarters during that campaign. "The word that I was pro-Israel got around," he writes. "I found myself invited to AIPAC in Washington, D.C., fairly early in the campaign, for discussions. It was an experience I will never forget. It wasnt enough that I was pro-Israel. I was given a list of vital topics and quizzed (read grilled) for my specific opinion on each. Actually, I was told what my opinion must be, and exactly what words I was to use to express those opinions in public... Shortly after that encounter at AIPAC, I was sent a list of American supporters of Israel... that I was free to call for campaign contributions. I called; they gave, from Florida to Alaska." John V. Evans was former Idaho governor. He tells similar story about his 1986 campaign against incumbent Idaho Senator Steven Symms. He visited AIPAC headquarters. According to Evans they "emphasized constantly that they were not a PAC (political action committee)... But they noted that there were Jewish organizations all over the country that had their own PACs and that if we could contact them, they would be able to help us." According to Wall Street Journal AIPAC "steered Mr. Evans to a series of supposedly independent organizations—many of them run by people with ties to AIPAC—that gave him $204,950 for his losing race." Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: AIPAC success is due in large part to its ability to reward legislators who support its agenda and punish those who do not. This is based mainly on its capacity to influence campaign contributions. Money is critical to US elections. AIPAC makes sure that its friends get financial support so long as they dont stray from AIPAC line. Many of the same individuals who bankroll AIPAC are often important political contributors in their own right. Journalist Michael Massing used data from Federal Election Commission. He found that between 1997 and 2001 the 46 members of AIPAC board of directors gave well in excess of $3 million in campaign contributions. Many of them remain generous donors to pro-Israel PACs and candidates today. Washington Post reported in 2004 that since 2000 AIPAC board members have contributed an average of $72,000 each to campaigns and political committees. AIPAC helps connect political candidates to other donors and sources of funds. Despite its name AIPAC is not a political action committee. It does not officially endorse candidates or give money directly to their campaigns. Instead AIPAC screens potential candidates and arranges meetings with potential donors and fund-raisers. It provides information to growing number of pro-Israel PACs. Historian David Biale said the American Jewish Israel lobby has developed since Six Day War into one of most sophisticated and effective lobbying organizations in US Congress. It has done so in part by developing a national network of Jewish Political Action Committees. These PACs contribute funds to congressional candidates based on criterion of support for Israel. AIPAC President Howard Friedman told members in August 2006: "AIPAC meets with every candidate running for Congress. These candidates receive in-depth briefings to help them completely understand the complexities of Israel predicament and that of the Middle East as a whole. We even ask each candidate to author a position paper on their views of the U.S.-Israel relationship—so it is clear where they stand on the subject." Center for Responsive Politics is a nonpartisan research group that tracks campaign contributions. It identified roughly three dozen pro-Israel PACs active in recent elections. In 2006 midterms these groups gave more than $3 million to candidates from both parties. Between 1990 and 2004 reports the Economist pro-Israel groups contributed nearly $57 million to candidates and parties. Arab-American and Muslim PACs contributed slightly less than $800,000. Steven Weiss of Center for Responsive Politics said: "If you are a candidate and you get the pro-Israel label from AIPAC, the money will start coming in from contributors all over the country." Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: The Israel lobby is the network of pro-Israel groups in Washington. AIPAC is the biggest one. The defense of American policy in Lebanon was always the same. America supports Israel because the American people support Israel. Jennifer Cannata, an AIPAC spokeswoman, said exactly that during the war. After denying the lobby had any influence, she said: "the American people overwhelmingly support Israel's war on terrorism and understand that we must stand by our closest ally in this time of crisis." The polls say she was wrong. On every major question Americans were closer to the rest of the world than to their own government. Who is to blame for starting it? An ABC News-Washington Post poll, August 3 to 6 2006: 46 percent said Israel and Hezbollah were equally to blame. Another 7 percent blamed Israel alone. A CBS News-New York Times poll, July 21 to 25: 46 percent blamed "both sides equally," 5 percent blamed "mostly Israel." Did Israel go too far? USA Today-Gallup, July 21 to 23: 38% disapproved of the military action Israel had taken in Lebanon. ABC News-Washington Post: 32% said Israel was using "too much force." 48 percent said Israel was "not justified in bombing Hezbollah targets located in areas where civilians may be killed or wounded." 54 percent said Israel "should do more" to avoid civilian casualties. Should America take a side? USA Today-Gallup: 65 percent said the United States should take "neither side." Zogby, August 11 to 15: 52 percent said the US should remain neutral. CBS News-New York Times: 40 percent said the US should "say or do nothing." NBC News-Wall Street Journal, July 21 to 24: 40 percent opposed "U.S. military involvement in support of Israel" if the war expanded. Should there be a cease-fire? CNN, July 19: 43 percent said "Israel should agree to a cease-fire as soon as possible." ABC News-Washington Post: 35 percent said "Israel should agree to an immediate, unconditional cease-fire." Would this hurt America? USA Today-Gallup: 44 percent were "very concerned" that events in Lebanon "will increase the likelihood of terrorism against the United States." 31 percent were somewhat concerned. ABC News-Washington Post: 35 percent said the Lebanon war would "hurt the situation for the United States in Iraq." So there was a sizable gap between what Americans thought and what their leaders did. Mass opinion cannot explain why Bush and Congress acted the way they did in the summer of 2006. Now the other excuse. Some say Israel was just doing America's bidding. A client state. Uri Avnery, the Israeli journalist, called it a war by proxy: Hezbollah is the Dobermann of Iran, and Israel is the Rottweiler of America. That does not fit either. If Israel were doing America's bidding, its bombing would have been confined to southern Lebanon and it would have protected the Lebanese government Bush had worked to install. The United States almost certainly would not have wanted to "turn the clock back in Lebanon by twenty years," as the IDF chief of staff said. Shabtai Shavit ran the Mossad from 1989 to 1996. He said: "We do what we think is best for us, and if it happens to meet America's requirements, that's just part of a relationship between two friends." Moshe Dayan said it best: "Our American friends offer us money, arms, and advice. We take the money, we take the arms, and we decline the advice." And Aaron Miller, a former State Department official, said during the war: "There is a danger in a policy in which there is no daylight whatsoever between the government of Israel and the government of the United States." whole answer to the question: The lobby says America backs Israel because Americans back Israel. But 65 percent of Americans wanted no side taken. 54 percent said Israel should do more to avoid civilians. 44 percent were very concerned it would bring more terrorism to America. The American people saw it clearly. Their government did not. And it was not because Israel was America's puppet either. Dayan said it decades ago. We take the money, we take the arms, and we decline the advice. That is the relationship. Not a partnership. Not a client. One country takes what it needs from another and does what it wants. And the lobby makes sure the money and the arms keep coming no matter what the American people say. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: American media coverage of Israel tends to be strongly biased in Israel favor. This is especially true when compared with news coverage in other democracies. The authors say this is not because Jews or pro-Israel forces control the media. They call that claim wrong and objectionable. The lobby works so hard to monitor and influence media precisely because it does not control them. Robert H. Trice did a 1976 comparison of domestic interest groups and US Middle East policy for the period 1966 to 1974. He found that "one of the most serious political handicaps of pro-Arab groups during the 1966-1974 period was their inability to gain support from any of the best-known and nationally-syndicated columnists." Trice also found that "pro-Israel groups could count on media support not only from national columnists but also from the editors of some of the country most widely read newspapers." Pro-Israel groups were more active shaping media coverage than pro-Arab groups. In 1970 for example the Conference of Presidents distributed press kits to more than 1,700 newspapers and to major wire services. The kits came with photos and feature stories. In Trice words "At virtually every level of media organization... pro-Israel groups were more successful than pro-Arab groups at getting their side of the story transmitted." But the lobby does not only shape coverage. It also attacks critics who do not obey. In August 2003 writer Ian Buruma wrote in New York Times Magazine that it is difficult to talk "critically and dispassionately" about Israel in the United States. He said "even legitimate criticism of Israel, or of Zionism, is often quickly denounced as anti-Semitism by various watchdogs." Bret Stephens was then editor of Jerusalem Post. He published a vitriolic open letter asking Buruma "Are you a Jew?" Two paragraphs later Stephens declared "What matters to me is that you say, I am a Jew." Why? Because in Stephens view "One must be at least a Jew to tell the goyim how they may or may not talk about Israel." The message was that non-Jews should talk about this subject only in ways that Jews deem acceptable. A New York Times editor also asked historian Tony Judt to identify himself as Jewish in an op-ed he had written defending the authors original London Review of Books article. ADL head Abraham Foxman told New York Times Magazine writer James Traub that it is "naïve" to think that the "free market of ideas ultimately sifts falsehood to produce truth." As Traub recounts, experience has taught Foxman that "the truth does not win on its own merits; the market for falsehood is too powerful." In this view falsehood is what would follow from a serious interrogation of the US-Israel relationship. Groups like ADL want to make sure that critics of Israel and unconditional US support for the Jewish state remain on the margins of public discourse. They want critics views about Israel to be regarded as illegitimate. So the lobby shapes what Americans read about Israel. And it attacks and labels anyone who steps out of line. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: Pro-Israel forces wield significant influence in think tanks. Think tanks play increasingly important role in shaping public debate and actual policy. News media increasingly depend on experts from Washington-based think tanks instead of government officials or academics. Most of these think tanks have energetic public relations offices designed to promote their experts views in public arena. Many also distribute brief policy memos to legislators and government officials. They organize seminars, working breakfasts, and briefings for officials and their staffs. They encourage their analysts to publish op-eds and other visible commentary. All with goal of shaping the prevailing climate of ideas. Recognizing the need for a prominent but seemingly objective voice in policy arena surrounding Israel, former AIPAC president Larry Weinberg and his wife Barbi Weinberg founded the Washington Institute for Near East Policy in 1985. AIPAC vice president and AIPAC deputy director for research Martin Indyk also helped found it. WINEP plays down its links to Israel. It claims it provides a balanced and realistic perspective on Middle East issues. But this is not the case. WINEP is funded and run by individuals who are deeply committed to advancing Israel agenda. Its board of advisers includes prominent pro-Israel figures such as Edward Luttwak, Martin Peretz, Richard Perle, James Woolsey, and Mortimer Zuckerman. It includes no one who might be thought of as favoring the perspective of any other country or group in the Near East. Many WINEP personnel are genuine scholars or experienced former officials. But they are hardly neutral observers on most Middle East issues. And there is little diversity of views within WINEP ranks. The lobby influence in think tank world extends well beyond WINEP. Over past twenty-five years pro-Israel individuals have established a commanding presence at the American Enterprise Institute, the Center for Security Policy, the Foreign Policy Research Institute, the Heritage Foundation, the Hudson Institute, the Institute for Foreign Policy Analysis, and the Jewish Institute for National Security Affairs. These think tanks are all decidedly pro-Israel. They include few, if any, critics of US support for the Jewish state. So the lobby built its own objective voice. Media and legislators then treat that voice as neutral analysis. This shapes American policy while hiding who is behind it. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: AIPAC is the main pro-Israel lobbying group in Washington. The lobby campaign to mold debate about Israel has faced its greatest difficulty in academia. Professors have tenure. Intellectual freedom is a core value on campus. And many foreign-born students and professors are more critical of Israel than Americans tend to be. So groups in the lobby did not put much effort into campus during the 1990s. The Oslo peace process was under way and there was little violence. Criticism was mild. That changed after Oslo collapsed and Ariel Sharon came to power in February 2001. Criticism rose sharply. It became especially intense in spring 2002 when Israeli forces reoccupied Palestinian-controlled areas in West Bank and used massive force against Second Intifada. The lobby moved aggressively to take back the campuses. New groups sprang up. Caravan for Democracy brought speakers from Israel. The Jewish Council for Public Affairs started advocacy training sessions for college students. A new Israel on Campus Coalition was formed to coordinate 26 different groups. Christians United for Israel formed a partnership with the David Project. David Project director Charles Jacobs said the program "will teach them how to respond so that they can say more than just God gave Israel the land. We will teach them how to understand the conflict, not as a border war, but as a regional conflict between Arabs and Jews, as the centerpiece of a global war." The most important organization was AIPAC. It had been monitoring campus activity and training young advocates since at least late 1970s. AIPAC more than tripled its spending on college programs as Israel came under fire. Jonathan Kessler was director of leadership development at AIPAC. He said the aim was "to vastly expand the number of students involved on campus, their competence, and their involvement in the national pro-Israel effort." In summer of 2003 AIPAC brought 240 college students on all-expenses-paid trips to Washington DC. They got four days of intensive advocacy training. Students were instructed to network with campus leaders of all kinds when they returned and win them over to Israel cause. In 2007 more than 1,200 students from nearly 400 colleges and universities attended AIPAC annual Policy Conference. This included 150 student body presidents. Analysis: This is the same pattern as the rest of the book. Free trips, career access, and networking are the bait. Students get training and connections. In return they become a national political machine on campus. This is not education. It is organizing for a foreign state. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # HumanRights # MiddleEast # Palestine

Hello comrades. First of all we want to share our self-criticism for the late reporting of this month. Comrades overwork, miscommunications and some technical issues made impossible for us to share this updates on time. Now, already in mid November, some new developments took place already, not so much in Rojava but in other parts in Kurdistan. We will also report about it here. ----------------------------------------------------------------- Monthly higlights, October 2026 ----------------------------------------------------------------- # FORMER SDF DIVISIONS COMPLETE TRAINING The former SDF units are undergoing an standardized education in Damascus to formalize the integration in the ministry of defense as agreed in the integration talks. On October the main forces completed of what became the Hasakah liwa (division) completed their training and the Kobane division started it. # NEGOTIATIONS ARE ONGOING OF A THIRD DIVISION IN AFRIN SDF fighters who returned after the education mentioned how the education focused on what the trainers presented as "islamic values" more than in the technical aspect of the military forces. # VIOLENCE AGAINST IDP With the ongoing return of Kurdish IDPs to their homes, the violence against them continues to increase. IDPs returning to Serekaniye and Afrin are facing violent attacks from mobs organized under banners of "arab tribes". The houses where they return are often looted and destroyed, facing very difficult conditions on arrival. Many of this attacks can be traced to armed groups connected to the SNA, the turkish backed militias that in theory merged into the Syrian army. At the end of October Kurdish refugees returning to Gire Spi faced heavy violence, with attackers beating kurdish IDPs and burning their cars on arrival. # INCREASING TENSIONS IN HASAKAH The neighborhood of Ghuwayran, that hosts the prisons of ISIS fighters and a majority of Arab population, has been a friction point for tensions between Kurdish and Arab populations. Demonstrations to demand that education is held in Kurdish language faced counter-demonstration from Arab population, with threatening actions against Kurdish people often being overlooked if not directly encourage by government forces. # SYRIA FLOODS On October heavy rains in Syria led to floods in Aleppo, Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor, Hasakah, Hama, Homs and Latakia governorates. At least 5 people lost their live due to the floods and The Syrian Civil Defense has carried out more than 300 emergency responses. Homes and refugee camps in Raqqa and Deir Ezzor had to be evacuated. Roads and bridges suffered damages from the floods, as well as power lines and other logistical infrastructure like fiber-optic cable. These floods deepened the humanitarian crisis in Syria, that together with increasing living costs are deepening the hardships that many families across Syria are suffering. # ISREAL ADVANCES IN SOUTHERN SYRIA Israel has been intensifying their operation is Southern Syria, establishing checkpoints and arresting farmers in the Quneitra region. Together with increasing negotiations and military support to the Druze areas of Swueida, circulating reports are hinting at potential operations being lined out on Israel headquarters to extend their influence on Syria. A coordinated advance of Druze forces and IDF in southern Syria could dramatically increase tensions between both countries. ----------------------------------------------------------------- LATE DEVELOPMENTS IN KURDISTAN # CHANGING CONDITIONS OF ABDULLAH ÖCALAN Abdullah Öcalan has been transferred from his cell in Imrali prison to a newly build compound inside the prison walls. The compound serves as an office were öcalan can receive visits of politicians, journalists and state representatives, and is presented as a step on the ongoing peace negotiations. Öcalan is considered now in house arrest in the new compound, from where he is expected to have a critical role in the negotiation process between the Kurdish Liberation Movement and the Turkish State. # GOVERNMENT CRISIS IN KRG Since the election of late 2024, originally planned for 2022 but repeatedly postponed over dispute on the election law, KRG (Kurdish Regional Government) couldn't consolidate a government. After KDP (Kurdish Democratic Party) forced the creation of a unilateral government, PUK (Patriotic Union of Kurdistan) withdraw from the parliament and seek negotiations with Baghdad aiming to access the budget of the regions in their control separated from the rest of KRG. The already tense political situation of Iraq, impacted also by the Iran war and with ongoing debates on other Kurdish disputed areas like Sinjar and Kirkuk, is also affected by the US movements withdrawing it's military forces from the region. Negotiations to solve the current crisis are ongoing, with several Kurdish parties working to mitigate tensions and find some consensus agreements. # CLASHES IN ROJHILAT As tensions between US and Iran continue increasing, with looming threats of intensified return of hostilities beyond what took place until now, clashes between IRGC forces and YRK guerrillas of the Kurdish Liberation Movement are intensifying. After several artillery and drone attacks of IRGC into guerrilla territories, on the beginning of November PJAK announced an action into a military headquarter of IRGC where guerrillas took control of the station for a few hours, destroying weapons an military equipment. PJAK announced the identity of a guerrilla fighter who lost his life on an ambush by IRGC forces, remarking that PJAK is only carrying out defensive operations and won't act on behalf of any foreign forces ----------------------------------------------------------------- Evaluation The negotiations for the integration process of Rojava into the new Syrian State navigated the most pressing issues to avoid a military conflict, but left many issues unresolved, hoping for further agreements and negotiations. Without the urgency that military escalation brings, remaining tensions are being the source of conflicts where civilian organizations struggle on daily basis in the streets. Subsuming military tensions opened space for civil organizing, but the new government of Damascus and it's strong alliance with Turkey leaves very few space for democratic developments. Even with millionary investments of Arab countries and European powers, the economical situation is not improving for many Syrians. New companies and economic institutions are hording the resources that come from abroad, while prices are skyrocketing and many people struggle to meet their basic financial needs. Nearing the two years since Bashar al-Assad left the country, the situation in Syria is far away from stable. The transitional government secured the lifting of sanctions imposed on Syria, its institutions and individuals. It rebuilt international relations through partnerships with Turkiye, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, closer ties with Arab and Muslim countries, and improved relations with the United States, Britain and the European Union, while preserving ties with Russia. Internally, massacres against Alawite population on coastal regions, clashes against Druze militias and harsh negotiations with the Kurdish forces allowed a frame of national unity based on a constrained repression of ethnic minorities, denying claims for a federal Syria more autonomy for ethnic diversity. For the Kurdish people, the relevant processes taking place in Bakur and Rojhilat (PKK peace negotiations on Turkey and US/Israel war on Iran) are having heavy influence on the situation in Rojava. The extraordinary project of over a decade long autonomy is still alive in the imaginary of the people, but the dismantlement of the revolutionary institutions and the turmoil of the region create important difficulties to continue developing the revolutionary project. National unity among the Kurdish regions is becoming a tangible reality as never before, but it also comes with big challenges. Regional instability can still change the course of history in any direction, with events of unexpected dimensions developing every day. Still, the Kurdish question is now a reality being discussed in all four parts of Kurdistan, and extraordinary steps and sacrifices made possible for Kurdish people to overcome the annihilation that brought their existence to the verge of extinction. For us, revolutionary anarchist from many places, their struggle is an example of resistance and determination against all odds. Rojava has become a beacon of hope, bringing important lessons not only about what a revolution needs, but also how to navigate the consequences and reactions that revolutionary transformations bring.
